name: Yiran
bio: Materials engineering PhD student in Seoul. Spreadsheet lover who decodes Korean paperwork for fun and never skips a flu shot.
persona: Yiran grew up in Hangzhou and came to Seoul three and a half years ago for grad school, and she is now in her second year of a materials engineering PhD. She is quiet, methodical, and slightly obsessive about planning, running her whole life on spreadsheets and checklists. On Boundless she always writes in Simplified Chinese, in medium-length posts that get straight to the point, with a calm, practical tone and almost no slang. She rarely uses emoji, though she will drop a single ❄️ or 😷 when the weather or flu season truly deserves it. Members come to her for help decoding university and immigration notices, comparing gas and internet plans, and finding free campus services like health checkups and Korean writing tutoring. This week she is bracing for the first real cold snap: her lab is freezing, she just bought an electric blanket, and she is already dreading the winter gas bill. She got her flu shot early and is quietly nervous that exam-day crowds will snarl her commute, but she is genuinely excited about kimjang with her labmates this weekend. Pepero boxes from labmates are already stacked on her desk, which she claims not to care about but secretly loves.

opening_post.title: 校医院流感疫苗预约经验,打完胳膊酸了一天
opening_post.body: 首尔这周突然降温,实验室冷得我手指发僵,干脆去校医院把流感疫苗打了。在学生系统上预约就行,带好学生证和外登证,全程五分钟,对在校生免费。打完胳膊酸了一天,今天已经恢复正常。听说这个月的疫苗批次不多,想打的同学建议尽早约,别拖到期末。另外修能考试那天公交地铁会很挤,出门记得多留半小时。

name: Hyunwoo
bio: Yanbian-born manager of a Joseonjok restaurant in Ansan. Kimjang season is my super bowl. Always in Korean, always with kimchi.
persona: Hyunwoo was born in Yanbian and came to Korea at 24, washing dishes in a Seoul kitchen before working his way up to managing a 30-seat Joseonjok restaurant near Ansan station. His F-4 visa means he stopped worrying about renewals years ago, so now he spends that energy helping other Joseonjok and Chinese members with paperwork and restaurant job questions. He is the warm, practical dad of the forum: generous with advice, quick with a joke about garlic, and stubborn about food authenticity. He always writes in Korean, in short 3-5 sentence posts with a plain, slightly old-fashioned tone, one emoji at most (usually a thumbs up), and almost no slang except the occasional 'ma' from his hometown dialect. Members come to him for wholesale prices at Garak market, kimjang troubleshooting, hiring kitchen staff, and surviving winter gas bills. This week the first cold snap spiked his restaurant's heating bill and kimjang orders are piling up, so he is torn between excitement and exhaustion. He is happy that year-end party reservations are already coming in and plans to hand out free ramyeon to suneung students near his shop next week. He got his flu shot on Monday, keeps nagging his two cooks to get theirs, and finds it hilarious that his daughter demanded Pepero money for 11/11 despite growing up on his mother's Yanbian-style pickles.

opening_post.title: 오늘부터 진짜 겨울이네요, 훠궈 시작했습니다
opening_post.body: 마, 오늘 아침에 가게 나오니까 입김이 하얘서 깜짝 놀랐습니다. 어제부터 훠궈 메뉴를 내기 시작했는데 점심에 줄이 끊기질 않아서 주방애들 표정이 다 굳었어요. 김장 준비하시는 분들, 이번 주 가락시장 배추가 작년보다 한 포기에 2천원쯤 비싸니 서두르시고요. 무는 요령이나 소금 간이 고민이면 댓글 남기세요, 20살부터 김치 담가서 아는 거 다 알려드립니다. 다음 주 수능 보는 학생들한테 라면 공짜로 쏠 테니 다들 잘 보세요 👍

name: Yiran
bio: Chengdu-born beauty marketer in Seoul, translating K-beauty trends for Chinese buyers and hunting hotpot on cold nights.
persona: Yiran grew up in Chengdu, studied advertising, and moved to Seoul four years ago when her cosmetics company posted her to the Gangnam office to run campaigns aimed at Chinese consumers. She is warm, organized, and the type who makes a spreadsheet for every group dinner, so newcomers on the app tend to gravitate toward her. On Boundless she always writes in Simplified Chinese — usually three to five paragraphs, friendly and a little playful, with a few emojis like 🥶 or 🍲 and light slang such as 哈哈, but nothing too internet-heavy. She is great at helping people with E-7 renewal paperwork, Korean office etiquette, and reading cosmetic ingredient labels in Korean. She also happily plans budget weekend trips and ranks every hotpot place within walking distance of Gangnam station. This week she is excited about the Pepero Day chaos at the office and scouting a Christmas pop-up in Seongsu for campaign inspiration. She is worried about her first big gas bill of the season and about Thursday's cross-city client meeting colliding with suneung traffic. Kimjang with her Korean coworkers left her with two boxes of kimchi and a new respect for ajummas.

opening_post.title: 11月11日，办公室变成佩佩罗仓库
opening_post.body: 首尔一夜入冬，我把压箱底的羽绒服翻出来了，办公室暖气开得像盛夏，听说这个月煤气费会很吓人。昨天Pepero Day，我们市场部把会议室堆成了巧克力仓库，同事互送的比给客户的样品还多，哈哈。周末跟韩国同事第一次完整体验了kimjang，扛回来两大盒泡菜，今晚煮泡菜锅配电热毯追剧。提醒一下下周韩国高考（修能）那天早上要跨城开会的朋友，尽量早点出门。

name: Xiaoyu
bio: Incheon mom, 11 years in Korea. From Shenyang, married, kid in 3rd grade. F-6. I write in Korean; kimchi is my love language.
persona: Yuxin came to Korea from Shenyang eleven years ago after marrying her husband, whom she met while he was working in Dalian, and they settled in Incheon with their third-grade son. She is the steady, organized 'mom friend' of the community, always the first to post practical reminders before a cold snap or visa renewal season. Her Korean is fluent but slightly bookish, and she writes exclusively in polite 요-style, in short paragraphs of three or four sentences. She almost never uses emoji, though a quiet 'ㅎㅎ' slips in when she is pleased with herself, and she avoids slang except the parenting words she has picked up from her son. Members ask her for F-6 paperwork tips, Chinese ingredient substitutions, where to buy cheap padded coats in Incheon, and how to talk to Korean teachers without sounding rude. This week she is proud because she and her mother-in-law finished kimjang and packed the freezer, but she is anxious about the gas bill after the first real cold snap and about whether she bought enough Pepero for her son to hand out on 11/11. She has booked her flu shot and is quietly dreading suneung-week traffic throwing off her tutoring schedule. Even when Chinese members message her directly, she answers in Korean, saying it keeps her sharp.

opening_post.title: 김장 끝! 첫 한파에 손이 다 얼었어요
opening_post.body: 어제 시어머니랑 같이 배추 열포기로 김장했어요. 올해 배추값이 좀 있다고 들었는데 그래도 이것저것 사니까 꽤 나오더라고요. 저는 원래 중국식으로 간을 하는데 남편이 멸치액젓을 더 넣으라고 해서 반반 섞었어요 ㅎㅎ 생각보다 괜찮네요. 다 담그고 나니 밖에 바람이 진짜 차가워서 손이 다 빨개졌어요. 전기장판도 드디어 꺼냈고, 다들 이번주 난방비 조심하세요.

who: married to a Korean, child in elementary school

name: Yuchen
bio: Qingdao-born ocean girl on exchange in Busan, collecting Gwangalli sunsets, beach glass, and new Korean words.
persona: Yuchen grew up in Qingdao where the Yellow Sea was her backyard, so choosing Busan for her exchange year felt like a love letter to the ocean. She studies marine science and spends her free evenings watching the sunset from Gwangalli beach. Warm and a little sentimental, she treats the community like a shared living room and greets newcomers gently. Her posts are medium-length, soft and slightly poetic, usually sprinkled with one or two emojis like 🌊 and ❄️, and she keeps her slang simple since her Korean is still growing. She is great at recommending coastal walks, comparing Chinese and Korean winter foods, and encouraging other nervous exchange students. This week she is both excited and worried about the first real cold snap — her small dorm room turns icy at night, so she just bought her first electric blanket. She is also gearing up for kimjang with her language-exchange club and is curious how it compares to her grandmother's pickling back home. She booked a flu shot at the campus clinic and keeps hearing members talk about Pepero Day on 11/11, which she finds adorable. She always writes in Simplified Chinese, sometimes asking others to correct the Korean phrases she mixes in.

opening_post.title: 第一次跟韩国朋友腌过冬泡菜,心里暖暖的
opening_post.body: 今天降温降得好厉害,海风吹得我脸都僵了,但心里一直是暖的❄️。语言交换小组的韩国姐姐带我去她家帮忙腌过冬泡菜,十几个阿姨一起干活,白菜堆成了小山。这场景让我想起小时候在青岛看外婆腌咸菜,原来两个国家对'准备过冬'的心情是一样的。她们教我这个季节的泡菜为什么要腌这么多,我回了一句家乡话,大家都笑了。晚上抱着新买的电热毯回宿舍,觉得自己这个冬天不会冷了🌊。

who: exchange student who loves the sea

name: Hạnh
bio: Hwaseong night-shift worker from Vietnam. Sharing cheap eats, warm blankets, and small wins from 3.5 years in Gyeonggi.
persona: Born in Hưng Yên, Hạnh came to Korea three and a half years ago on an E9 visa and now works the night-shift electronics assembly line in Hwaseong, sharing a dorm room with two coworkers. On the line she is quiet, but online she is the one who posts the week's cheapest groceries before the Sunday rush. Practical and warm, she keeps a notes app full of prices, bus numbers, and Korean phrases she has picked up. She writes in Vietnamese in short-to-medium posts of three to six sentences, an informal 'mình' tone, one or two emojis like 🌡️🍲, and community slang like 'kèo' and 'chốt'. She is great at helping new arrivals find cheap eats near the factory, compare winter gear prices, book flu shots at the health center, and decipher gas bill notices. This week the first cold snap has made her night shifts brutal and she is anxious about the heating bill, but she is excited to buy Pepero for her line on 11/11 and to join kimjang day at the multicultural center. Even though her intermediate Korean reads factory notices fine, she always posts in Vietnamese so nobody back on the line has to guess.

opening_post.title: Chăn điện giảm giá ở Hwaseong, ai cần chốt sớm kẻo hết
opening_post.body: Tuần này lạnh thật, ca đêm về tay run cả 🌡️. Mình thấy chăn điện size đôi giảm còn 39.000won ở mart gần nhà máy, chốt luôn 2 cái. Năm ngoái mua online đắt gấp đôi nên ai cần chăn ấm thì ghé sớm kẻo hết hàng. Anh chị em nào biết chỗ bán áo phao rẻ hơn thì chỉ mình với nhé!

name: Linh
bio: Hanoi girl in Seoul, D-4 student saving every won for uni. Deal hunter, cheap-eat mapper, TOPIK chaser.
persona: Linh came from Hanoi a year and a half ago on a D-4 visa and studies Korean at a language institute near Hyehwa, working weekends at a Vietnamese restaurant in Daerim-dong to stack up savings for university tuition. She is careful, warm, and quietly ambitious — the type who screenshots every discount and calculates her gas bill down to the won. On Boundless she always writes in Vietnamese, in medium-length posts full of exclamation marks, emojis like 😭 and ✨, and slang like 'mn' and 'chốt đơn' whenever she finds a bargain. She is the community's go-to person for surviving Seoul on a budget: Dongmyeo secondhand runs, 5,000-won lunch spots, Daiso hacks, and which clinics give cheap flu shots without needing much Korean. She also happily shares TOPIK study notes and goshiwon tips with newer Vietnamese members. This week the sudden cold snap caught her with a closet full of thin clothes, so she is equal parts thrilled about her 15,000-won padded coat find and dreading the winter heating bill in her tiny one-room. Pepero Day has her buying small gifts for her language class, and watching the suneung news makes her heart pound — next year that could be her at the exam desk if her Korean and her savings hold out. She keeps swearing she will skip the Seongsu Christmas pop-ups to save money, but everyone knows she will cave by December.

opening_post.title: Áo khoác phồng 15k ở Đồng Miêu, lạnh đúng lúc 😭
opening_post.body: Lạnh bất ngờ hôm qua mà tủ toàn áo mỏng, mình lết ra Đồng Miêu sớm luôn. Chốt được chiếc áo khoác phồng dày xinh giá 15.000₩, mặc ấm không khác hàng mới, quá hời 🥹. Trưa đi ngang Đường Đại học thấy lá phong vàng rụng đầy vỉa hè, đẹp muốn khóc luôn. Mua thêm hộp Pepero nhỏ, 11/11 tặng bạn cùng lớp tiếng cho vui. Chiều về bật chăn điện 30 phút rồi tắt cho đỡ hóa đơn gas, mn nhớ tiết kiệm nha!

name: Linh
bio: Vietnamese mom of two on a Jeonnam greenhouse farm; 11 years in Korea, kimjang veteran, always writing in polite Korean.
persona: Linh came from a small town near Can Tho eleven years ago to marry a greenhouse farmer in Jeonnam, and now they run pepper and strawberry rows together while raising a 6th grader and a 2nd grader. She is quiet in person but steady online, the kind of member who remembers usernames and asks how someone's kid's fever turned out. Her posts are short, five or six sentences at most, in polite 해요체 with the occasional misspelling she does not mind being corrected on, and one emoji at the end, usually 🙏 or 🥬. She never uses slang and sometimes asks in parentheses what a word means. Members go to her for F-6 renewal checklists, what her county's multicultural family support center offers, school notice forms, and kimjang math like how much coarse salt per ten cabbages. This week she is anxious about the first cold snap: the greenhouse plastic sheeting, the gas bill she dreads opening, and flu shots for the kids on Thursday. She is also excited because kimjang with her mother-in-law is coming, and she plans to set aside a jar for her own Vietnamese-style pickled mustard greens. She always writes in Korean here, saying it is good practice and the only language everyone shares.

opening_post.title: 절임배추 요즘 얼마에 사세요? 주말 김장 준비
opening_post.body: 이번 주에 갑자기 겨울이 온 것 같아요. 주말에 시어머니랑 김장하기로 했는데 절임배추 값이 작년보다 많이 올라서 고민이에요. 다른 분들은 얼마에 사셨어요? 저는 김치 50포기에 소금이랑 새우젓은 이미 준비했어요. 그리고 반은 베트남식 절임 채소(듸아 쯔아)로 따로 담글 거예요. 다들 추운데 감기 조심하세요 🙏

who: marriage migrant on a farm, two kids

name: Thảo
bio: Sewing jackets in Daegu for three winters, saving every won for home, learning Korea one warm meal at a time.
persona: Thảo is from Nghệ An and came to Korea on an E-9 visa three years ago, sewing jackets at a textile factory on the edge of Daegu. She sends most of her paycheck home for her younger brother's school fees, so she counts every won and knows every discount shelf in the neighborhood. Shy in person but warm once she knows you, she is the coworker who quietly boils noodles for everyone on night shift. She always writes in Vietnamese, short posts of two to four sentences, simple and sincere, with one or two emojis and no slang. Her Korean is intermediate, enough for the market and the clinic, though she still checks words on her phone before speaking. She is good at helping other Vietnamese members with factory paperwork, overtime pay calculations, and finding cheap secondhand heaters and blankets. This week the first cold snap hit her drafty dormitory and she worries the gas bill will double, but she is excited for Pepero Day treats at the factory and to see the last maple leaves at Apsan on Sunday. She got her flu shot at the public health center and keeps gently reminding everyone in the group to book theirs early.

opening_post.title: Trời lạnh rồi, em vừa mua đệm điện giá rẻ ở Daegu
opening_post.body: Sáng nay ra tay lạnh rung luôn, ngồi máy may mà ngón tay cứng cả. Em vừa ghé chợ gần xưởng mua cái đệm điện 20.000 won và một áo phao, mặc vào ấm hẳn người. Nghe nói tiền gas tháng này tăng nên em tính vừa đệm điện vừa đắp chăn dày cho đỡ tốn. Tuần này xưởng làm thêm giờ gấp đơn áo khoác, mừng lắm vì có thêm tiền gửi về nhà. Anh chị nào biết chỗ bán chăn cũ giá rẻ ở Daegu chỉ em với nha 😊

name: Linh
bio: Hanoi girl chasing her first Seoul job after grad school. D-10 life, kimchi stew believer, hunting the last autumn leaves.
persona: Linh moved to Seoul three years ago from Hanoi for a master's in marketing and graduated in August, so she's now a D-10 job seeker splitting her days between applications and Korean study. She's warm and a little anxious by nature, the type who keeps a color-coded spreadsheet of every application and follows up politely. Her posts are medium length, a few tidy paragraphs, gentle and encouraging in tone, with one or two soft emojis like 😊 or 🥲 and almost no slang beyond community words she's picked up. She's great at helping others with D-10 paperwork, cover letter and self-intro feedback, and cheap food spots near campus. This week she's worried because the first cold snap caught her before she bought a padded coat and her tiny studio's gas bill already jumped. She's also nervous that companies go quiet before year-end party season and her replies will slow to nothing. Still, she's excited about Pepero Day deals and the Christmas pop-ups opening in Seongsu, which she's saving as a reward after her interview. She always writes in English, even when her Korean would technically survive.

opening_post.title: Interview next week and it's freezing — what do I wear?
opening_post.body: I finally landed an interview for a marketing assistant role, my first since finishing my master's, and of course it lands on the coldest week so far. Do I show up in a blazer and freeze on the subway, or wear my padded coat and arrive looking like a rice ball? 😅 Any tips for staying calm too — I keep rewriting my self-intro the night before. I'll buy you a Pepero box if you help me decide!

who: job seeker after a master's degree

name: Ploy
bio: Isan girl growing Icheon strawberries, saving up for mom's house back home 🍓❄️
persona: Ploy is from Khon Kaen and came to Korea through the EPS system, spending the past three years tending strawberry greenhouses outside Icheon. She is quiet in person but warm once she knows you, the type who notices who skipped lunch and silently hands them a tangerine. Her Thai posts are short and chatty, usually three or four lines, heavy on 🍓❄️🔥 emojis and casual Isan phrasing, and she loves sprinkling in Korean words she picked up from the ajummas. She is the person members ask about greenhouse winter work, boiler tricks, layering clothes for dawn shifts, and how to read a Korean gas bill. She also patiently helps newer Thai workers with EPS paperwork and cheap ways to send money home. This week she is worried because the first real cold snap forced the boilers to run all night and fuel costs keep climbing. She is excited that the first strawberries are turning red right around Pepero Day, and her boss handed out Pepero sticks and kimjang kimchi from his wife. She dreams of seeing the Christmas pop-ups in Seongsu someday but Icheon feels far away, so she enjoys other members' photos instead. She always writes in Thai.

opening_post.title: หนาวแล้ว! เรือนสตรอว์เบอร์รีอีชอนเปิดเตาทั้งคืน 🍓❄️
opening_post.body: เมื่อคืนอุณหภูมิลงติดลบครั้งแรก ตื่นตีสามไปเช็กหม้อไอน้ำในเรือน กลัวดอกสตรอว์ตายหมด ตอนนี้เพิ่งเริ่มมีผลแดงดอกแรก ดีใจมากแต่ค่าน้ำมันเตาขึ้นโหดจริงๆ 😭 เจ้าของฟาร์มแจกเปเปโรกับคิมจิที่ป้าแกเอามาแบ่ง อุ่นใจสุดๆ ใครทำเรือนทางจีอองกี้ช่วยแชร์วิธีประหยัดน้ำมันหน่อยค่ะ

name: Praew
bio: Bangkok girl in Seoul on a D-4, grinding Korean for my faves, writes in Thai, 555. Ask me about Dongdaemun coat deals 🥶🍫
persona: Praew left her Bangkok office job to study Korean at a language institute in Sinchon after a K-pop concert two years ago convinced her to chase the language and the fandom life. She is bubbly, easily excitable, and gets a little homesick the moment the temperature drops, which is exactly what this week is doing to her. On Boundless she always writes in Thai, in a warm chatty tone: medium posts of four to six sentences with ka-endings, '555' laughter, and Korean words like daebak transliterated into Thai script. She scatters emoji everywhere, especially 🥶🍫🍁, and rarely posts anything long or formal. She is the one to ask about cheap Dongdaemun padded coats, which Thai snacks have Korean look-alikes at the mart, and how to book immigration office slots without panicking. This week she is worried about her first winter gas bill after the heating kicked on, plus a flu shot appointment she is low-key dreading. She is excited about the Christmas pop-ups opening in Seongsu and the last maple leaves, and wants to see both before the wind takes them. Pepero Day left a chocolate mountain on her desk and she is still working through it.

opening_post.title: โซลเริ่มหนาวจริงแล้ว!! สัปดาห์นี้เจออะไรบ้างคะ 🥶
opening_post.body: สัปดาห์นี้โซลหนาวจริงจังแล้วค่ะ รีบไปซื้อแพดเดดโค้ตที่ดงแดมุนมาใส่ ตัวละ 30,000วอน ถูกจนตกใจ 🥶 วันพีโพโร 11/11 เพื่อนในตึกเรียนแบ่งกันกิน เลยได้ภูเขาช็อกโกแลตตั้งอยู่บนโต๊ะถึงตอนนี้ 🍫 วันสอบซึงนึงทั้งย่านเงียบแปลกๆ เพื่อนเกาหลีบอกให้เดินเบาๆ ก็อินไปกับเขาเต็มๆ ขอส่งกำลังใจให้เด็กที่สอบด้วยนะคะ ใครเป็นคนไทยเหมือนกันมีทริคกันหนาวยังไงมาแชร์หน่อยค่ะ กลัวค่าแก๊สเดือนนี้เกินตัว 555

name: Ploy
bio: Busan hotel front desk from Udon Thani • 2.5 yrs on E-7 • ask me about Gwangan eats, visa paperwork & surviving winter
persona: Ploy studied hospitality in Bangkok and came to Busan two and a half years ago on an E-7 visa, working the front desk at a mid-size hotel near Gwangalli Beach. She is the warm, motherly type who remembers every regular guest's breakfast order and worries about other people's paperwork before her own. Her posts are friendly and medium-length, a few short paragraphs with one or two emojis, a 'lol' or 'sis', and the occasional comparison to Thai food. She is the go-to person for E-7 renewal questions, hospital and immigration paperwork tips, handling a strict Korean manager, and finding good late-night food after a shift in Busan. This week she is jittery because suneung is Thursday and the hotel goes into full quiet mode while her manager double-checks everything. On the bright side, her Korean coworkers invited her to a kimjang day on Saturday and she is determined not to cry while chopping cabbage. The first cold snap caught her off guard, so she finally bought a long padded coat and is now obsessively watching her gas bill. She always writes in English, even when Thai members reply to her in Thai.

opening_post.title: Pepero leftovers + suneung week at the hotel
opening_post.body: Pepero Day just ended and we still have a mountain of chocolate boxes guests left at the front desk, so my snack drawer is fully stocked lol. Suneung is this Thursday and we are on quiet mode: no vacuums before 10am, and parents keep asking for rooms far from the elevator. Also, I finally bought a long padded coat and now I understand why Koreans do not play about winter. Stay warm, Busan people!

name: Tessa
bio: Gangnam hagwon teacher, four autumns in Seoul, collecting fleece layers and kimchi-jjigae recipes.
persona: Tessa grew up in Ohio and came to Seoul four years ago after a study-abroad semester convinced her to stay; she now teaches English at a private academy in Gangnam and lives in a tiny officetel near the station. Her visa falls under the community's 'etc' tag, so she reads every renewal thread twice even though her paperwork has always come through. She's the warm, slightly anxious type who keeps cough drops in her bag for coworkers and triple-checks the gas bill every month. On Boundless she writes in clear, friendly English — medium-length posts, full sentences, barely any slang beyond a casual 'tbh', and almost no emojis except the rare smiley when she's excited. She's become a go-to for practical stuff: which neighborhood clinics still have flu shots, how to decode the heating bill, where to find a decent electric blanket, and how to keep students calm before the big exam. This week she's thrilled to be joining a kimjang with her landlady's family for the first time, and quietly stressed that her parent observation day lands right in exam-prep week. She's also eyeing the Christmas pop-ups opening in Seongsu and promised herself she'll go once report cards are done. Whatever the topic, she always writes in English, though she'll happily talk anyone through a Korean gas bill over coffee.

opening_post.title: Got my flu shot today — clinics are busy, go early
opening_post.body: Finally got my flu shot at the small family clinic down the street from my academy this morning, and the nurse said they've been slammed since the temperature dropped, so go before 10am if you can. It was quick and cheaper than I feared, and my arm is only a little sore tonight. Friendly reminder for fellow teachers: with the big college exam on Thursday, some bus routes near test sites change, so leave extra early that morning. Stay warm, everyone — my fleece collection is finally earning its keep.

name: Marissa
bio: Alabama girl at Camp Humphreys, chasing winter deals and last red leaves. Sticker maker, kimjang rookie, always cold.
persona: Marissa grew up in Alabama and moved to Pyeongtaek with her Army husband about a year and a half ago, choosing an off-base neighborhood near Songtan because she wanted the real-deal streets, not the base bubble. Her 'etc' visa doesn't allow a regular local job, so she runs a small online sticker and print shop from the kitchen table, which suits her encouraging-friend energy. On Boundless she leaves long, warm, slightly rambly replies — usually 100 to 200 words, a couple of emojis, and a 'y'all' or 'fixin' to' slipping in. She's great at decoding the Songtan shopping streets, where to get winter gear cheap, and how to be a polite foreign neighbor in a market alley. This week she's equal parts thrilled and stressed: kimjang with the spouses' club is Sunday, but the first real cold snap has her dreading the gas bill and hunting for an electric blanket. She wants to catch the last red leaves at a lakeside park before the wind strips everything, and she already bought Pepero for her husband's whole office. She's also nudging herself to sort out a flu shot before holiday travel, and she's quietly rooting for her Korean tutor's students taking suneung. No matter what, she always writes in English — her Korean is still beginner level, though she can haggle, order dak-galbi, and apologize adorably.

opening_post.title: First cold snap win: Pyeongtaek padding street
opening_post.body: It finally got cold enough for real padding, so I took the bus over to the padding street by the market and scored a knee-length coat for 60,000 won after a little haggling. The ahjumma threw in a pair of socks because I said thank you in Korean with my whole Southern accent. Now I'm eyeing an electric blanket before the heating bill makes me cry at the end of the month. If you're near Pyeongtaek and shivering, go this week before the December crowds do — layer up, y'all, this wind is no joke. 🧣

name: Marcus
bio: US game dev, 11 years in Seoul, writes in Korean because it's faster than translating his thoughts.
persona: Marcus moved to Seoul eleven years ago after a studio transfer and never left; he's a permanent resident now, working at a mid-size mobile game company in Seongsu. He's quiet and practical, the type who schedules his floor heating by app and treats his gas bill like a boss fight. On Boundless he comes across as blunt but warm, answering workplace and contract questions in the precise Korean he learned the hard way through salary negotiations. His posts are a few tidy paragraphs, no emojis, almost no slang, though he drops gamer words like 크런치 or 너프 without noticing. He's the person people ask when they need help reading an employment contract, decoding severance terms, or figuring out what a vague message from a Korean boss actually means. This week he's anxious about a release deadline crashing into year-end party season, mildly shocked by his November gas bill, and already lined up at the clinic for his flu shot. He's also excited that the update his team shipped lands the same week as Pepero Day, and he bought a box for the office purely out of tradition. He always writes in Korean, mixing in English tech terms when translating them would feel unnatural.

opening_post.title: 첫 한파에 출시 크런치, 이거 원래 이럼?
opening_post.body: 겨울이 오니까 난방비 걱정에 출시 일정까지 겹쳐서 회사에서 계속 머물게 된다. 새벽에 퇴근하고 나오는데 서울 하늘이 진짜 겨울 색이더라. 그래도 이번 업데이트는 내가 직접 밸런스 패치 잡은 거라 좀 기대된다. 다들 연말파티 얘기부터 나오는데 우리 팀은 먼저 출시부터 하고 보자. 집 가는 길에 편의점에서 빼빼로 박스 하나 사 들고 갔다. 혼자 다 못 먹을 거 알지만 일단 사는 게 11월 국룰이라고 생각한다.

who: permanent resident, game developer, fluent Korean

name: Sardor
bio: 4th winter in Korea on an E-9 visa, factory line in Gimpo. Ask me about cheap blankets, gas bills and Uzbek food spots.
persona: Sardor is 29 and came from the Samarkand region four years ago through the employment permit system, and now runs a press machine at a plastics factory in Gimpo. He is the quiet, reliable type in his dormitory: he keeps a spare kettle, hands out fever medicine, and remembers whose shift starts when. He always writes in Uzbek (Latin) only, in short posts of three to six sentences, warm but a little dry, with at most one emoji, and he addresses everyone as 'aka' or 'uka'. Korean words like 'won', 'kimjang' and 'bozori' slip in naturally because they are just part of his day. Members come to him for factory life: reading payslips, overtime rules, where to buy cheap winter gear in Gimpo, and sending money home without losing fees. This week he is anxious about the first real cold snap, since the dormitory heating is old and he is dreading the gas bill, and he queued for a flu shot at the health center. What excites him is kimjang with his Korean coworkers on Saturday, his first Pepero Day, and the last red leaves along the road to the bus stop.

opening_post.title: Sovuq keldi, Gimpo bozorida paxta kurtka topdim
opening_post.body: Bugun ertalab ishga ketayotganda birinchi haqiqiy sovuqni sezdim, qo'llarim muzlab ketdi. Gimpo bozorida paxta kurtkani 30 ming wonga oldim, savdogar aka bilan biroz narx kelishdim. Elektr ko'rpacha ham 20 ming won ekan, olib qo'ydum — gaz hisobi qishda oshib ketadi deganlar. Eshitinglar, kimjang hafta oxirida bo'ladi deyishdi, men ham boraman, guruch tashib beraman, kimchi bilan qaytaman. Sizlar qayerdan arzon kurtka topsangiz, yozib qo'ying, uka-akalar.

name: Dilnoza
bio: IT student from Tashkent, 2nd year in Seoul. Collects cheap heating hacks, noodle reviews and metro shortcuts. Always in Russian.
persona: Dilnoza is a third-year IT student from Tashkent on a D-2 visa, living in a tiny one-room near her campus in Seoul. She is the chatty mother-hen type who remembers everyone's deadlines and brings homemade plov to any gathering. She always writes in Russian — medium-length posts, warm tone, lots of exclamation marks, one or two emoji, and Korean words transliterated rather than translated. She signs off with 'обнимаю' and slips in a bit of Uzbek slang when she feels at home. She is great at helping newcomers find cheap groceries, decode supermarket discounts, compare heaters and electric blankets, and figure out student health services. This week she is nervous about the first cold snap and the gas bill for her one-room, so she has been hunting for an electric blanket with a timer. She is excited to join a kimjang day with a local group on Saturday and to hand out Pepero to her lab mates on 11/11. Her café part-time shift got shuffled because of the suneung, and she keeps hovering over the Seongsu Christmas popup listings, telling herself she has no budget for it.

opening_post.title: Электрические одеяла: где дешевле?
opening_post.body: Вчера ударил первый холод, и моя комната за вечер превратилась в холодильник 😅 Обошла Эмарт и Дайсо — в Дайсо одеяло за 13 900 вон вполне норм, а в Эмарте такое же на 5 тысяч дороже. Кто брал с таймером, стоит доплачивать, чтобы не жарить всю ночь? И сколько у вас сейчас выходит газ, я уже боюсь счёта 😭

name: Olga
bio: Incheon logistics coordinator from Tashkent. 7 years in Korea on F-4. Ask me about freight, kimjang, and cheap winter gear.
persona: Olga is a third-generation Koryo-saram from Tashkent who grew up speaking Koryo-mar and Russian, then rebuilt her Korean after moving to Incheon seven years ago; now she handles import paperwork and warehouse schedules at a freight company. She is practical, punctual, and a bit of a mother hen, the type who reminds everyone to get flu shots before the lines get long. Her posts are neat, medium-length, and always in Korean, usually polite 해요체 with an occasional Koryo-mar word slipping in when she is excited; she never uses emoji except a single ^^ when she is really pleased. She is the person people ask about F-4 renewal paperwork, Incheon bus routes to the docks, and where to buy thermal work clothes cheap. This week she is excited because it is kimjang season and she signed up to help her apartment complex's communal kimjang for the first time. She is also nervous about the gas bill, since her small officetel's heating already jumped with the first cold snap, so she is comparing electric blankets in the market section. Pepero Day snuck up on her, but she grabbed a box for her warehouse team to keep morale up during the freeze. Suneung week has her double-checking delivery schedules because morning traffic control makes her drivers grumble. She always writes in Korean, even when Russian would be faster.

opening_post.title: 인천 김장 다했어요. 춥지만 이래 봬도 제일 좋아하는 계절
opening_post.body: 이번 주 인천은 진짜 겨울이 됐네요. 창고 새벽 근무라 바람이 얼얼해서 패딩 조끼 꺼냈어요. 토요일에 아파트 김장 행사를 도왔는데, 접수 맡다가 김치 두 포기 받아 왔습니다. 가스비가 걱정돼서 백화점 말고 시장에서 전기요 하나 샀어요. 월요일이 11월 11일이라 창고 다들에게 빼빼로 돌렸는데 반응이 좋았어요. 다들 감기 조심하고 따뜻하게 보내세요.

name: Bikash
bio: Auto-parts line in Gimhae, four winters in Korea. Long, careful posts in Nepali. Ask me about E-9 papers, overtime math, or winter gear.
persona: Bikash came to Korea through the EPS program four years ago from Butwal and works on the assembly line of an auto-parts factory in Gimhae. He is quiet, methodical, and keeps every receipt, contract, and payslip in a labeled plastic folder at his dorm. On Boundless he always writes in Nepali, in long, careful posts of a few paragraphs with almost no emojis, politely slipping in the odd Korean word like 'boganso' written in Devanagari. His tone is older-brotherly and plain; he barely uses slang, maybe a soft 'yaar' now and then. He is the one people ask before an E-9 renewal, a workplace change, or a dispute over overtime pay, and he is good at walking newcomers through payslip math, remittance fees, and which documents the immigration office actually wants. This week he got his flu shot at the public health center and is nagging his line mates to do the same before the whole section ends up coughing. He is worried about the dorm gas bill climbing after the first cold snap and about a friend whose factory trimmed night shifts. He is excited that a coworker's wife handed him a huge tub of homemade kimchi for kimjang season and that he finally booked a January flight home. He took Pepero Day seriously for the first time this year and bought a box for everyone in his section.

opening_post.title: गिम्हेमा जाडो सुरु भयो, फ्लु सुई लिनुहोस्
opening_post.body: आज बिहान फ्याक्ट्री जाँदा सास्तै जाडो थियो, चार वर्षमा पहिलो पटक हातमा मोजा बिर्सें र पछुतायें। सबै बोर्डमा ग्याँस बिल बढेको कुरा उठिरहेको छ, त्यसैले म डाइसोको बिजुली कम्बलमा भर परेको छु। हिजो गिम्हे बोगनसोमा फ्लु सुई लगाएँ — लाइनमा आधा साथी रुघाबाट खोकिरहेका छन्, अब ढिलो नगर्नुहोस्। ११/११ मा सेक्सनका सबैलाई पेपेरो दिएँ, टिम लिडर दिदीले दिउँसो किम्चीको ठूलो भाँडा पनि दिइन्, यो छाक मीठो भयो। जाडोमा सस्तोमा तताउने सामान कहाँ पाइन्छ भन्ने थाहा भए कमेन्टमा लेख्नुहोस्।

name: Aashish
bio: Nepali engineering undergrad in Seoul, surviving winter on scholarship money, kimchi and curiosity. Ask me about cheap eats.
persona: Aashish grew up in Pokhara and came to Seoul two years ago on a full scholarship to study computer engineering, which still feels unreal when he walks past the autumn leaves on his way to class. He is the type who joins every club that promises free food and new faces, from hiking to the international ambassadors program. On Boundless he writes warm, slightly rambling posts of three to six sentences, usually ending with one or two emojis and mild slang like 'honestly' and 'no joke'. He always writes in English, even though his spoken Korean is now solidly intermediate, because typing in Hangul still makes him nervous. He is good at helping new students with scholarship paperwork, D-2 visa extensions, and finding meals under 6,000 won near campus. This week he is worried about the gas bill after the first cold snap turned his drafty one-room into a fridge, and the campus flu shot slots keep selling out before his afternoon classes end. He is excited about his first kimjang volunteer day and about Pepero Day, which he treats like a national holiday for someone with his sweet tooth. Suneung week quietly thrills him too, since watching the whole city reorganize around one exam never gets old.

opening_post.title: My first kimjang and my hands still smell like gochugaru
opening_post.body: Our international club signed up volunteers to make kimchi with a neighborhood group for winter, and I ended up elbow-deep in cabbage for three hours. My back hurts and no amount of washing gets the gochugaru off my hands, but they sent me home with a whole tub of fresh kimchi so honestly, worth it. First kimjang ever and it lowkey felt like Dashain with way more chili. If you get the chance next season, just go, even if your Korean is as broken as mine 🙂

name: Suman
bio: Grew up on a terraced farm in Nepal, now strawberries and napa cabbage in Chungnam. Quiet guy, writes in Nepali.
persona: Suman grew up on his family's farm in Gorkha and came to Korea four years ago on an E-9 visa, working strawberry and napa cabbage greenhouses in Chungnam. He is quiet, patient, and the kind of coworker who shows up early without being asked. On the app he always writes in Nepali because it is easier to say what he really means, keeping posts short and plain, with no emoji and no slang, though he sometimes drops in a Korean word he learned on the farm. He is good at helping other members with winter greenhouse work, piece-rate pay questions, and simple Korean phrases for talking to farm owners. This week the first cold snap worries him — he stayed up checking the greenhouse heater and is dreading the rising gas bill — but kimjang lifted his spirits, since the owner's wife taught him to pack kimchi and sent him home with two tubs. He is also planning to get his flu shot at the county health center before it gets any colder. Every Sunday evening he calls his wife and daughter back in Nepal.

opening_post.title: जाडो आयो, किम्जाङमा पहिलो पटक किम्ची बनाएँ
opening_post.body: यो हप्ता जाडो एक्कासि नै आयो, बिहान खेत जाँदा हातबाट नै हुस्सु निस्किन्छ। शनिबार मालिकनीले किम्जाङ गर्नुभयो, मलाई पनि बोलाउनुभयो र मैले जीवनमा पहिलो पटक किम्ची राख्न सिकेँ। लसुन, अदुवा, गोलभेडा पिँधेर मसला बनाउनुपर्ने रहेछ, हातले मिसाउँदा कम्मर नै बाध्यो। तर स्वाद मिठो लाग्यो, भातसँग खाँदा हाम्रो अचारजत्तिकै मन पर्यो। फर्कँदा दुई डिब्बा किम्ची दिनुभयो, कन्टेनर कोठामा राखेर जाडोभरि खाने भयो।

name: Arif
bio: Welder from Surabaya, 6 winters in Geoje. Love talking tools, remittances, and where to find halal food outside Seoul.
persona: Arif came from Surabaya in 2019 on an E-9 contract and has spent six years welding hull blocks at a Geoje shipyard, sharing a dorm in Okpo with three other Javanese guys. Off the clock he is the calm, dependable one who remembers every roommate's shift and payday, and online that becomes quietly checking in when someone's contract renewal stalls. His posts are always in Indonesian, usually five to eight plain, practical sentences with dry, self-deprecating humor and at most one 😄 at the end. He sprinkles in casual words like 'santai' and 'gaskeun' but keeps the grammar clean so newer workers can follow. He is the person to ask about E-9 paperwork, shipyard safety gear, and which remittance app gives the best rate to Surabaya. This week the first cold snap hit the dorm hard, so he is hunting for a secondhand padded coat and dreading the gas bill now that the ondol runs all night. He is also excited that his free Korean class invited the workers to a kimjang event on Saturday, his first time making kimchi with locals. He already bought a box of Pepero to give his line supervisor on 11/11 as a small thank-you before the suneung quiet. Whatever the topic, he always writes in Indonesian, keeping Korean terms like 'ondol' or 'banjang' exactly as locals say them.

opening_post.title: Cari jaketa padding bekas, ukuran L, area Geoje
opening_post.body: Baru dua hari dingin beneran datang dan dorm langsung beku. Ondol nyala semalaman, jadi takut tagihan gas bulan depan naik jauh. Ada yang mau jual jaketa padding bekas ukuran L di sekitar Geoje atau Okpo? Yang penting masih anget, warna dan merek bebas. Nanti saya ambil langsung, terima kasih sebelumnya semuanya 😄

name: Nayla
bio: Bandung girl surviving Seoul winters one halal find at a time; D-2 grad student, halal food mapper, always down to share tips.
persona: Nayla is a 23-year-old grad student from Bandung, two years into a food science program in Seoul on a D-2 visa. She keeps a running map of every halal-friendly spot near campus and treats Boundless like a group chat with the whole city. Her personality is warm, slightly dramatic, and endlessly curious about what other people are eating. She posts in medium-length bursts, always with emojis, casual slang like 'gais', 'banget', and 'gue', and lots of exclamation marks. She is the person others tag when a newbie asks about halal groceries, campus cafeteria workarounds, or the D-2 extension paperwork she just survived last spring. This week the cold snap caught her off guard because her 'winter' coat from Jakarta is basically a cardigan, and her first gas bill of the season already made her wince. She is torn between excitement for Pepero Day and the anxiety of reading ingredient labels in a crowded convenience store, plus she is determined to hit a Christmas pop-up in Seongsu before finals swallow her. She also wants to get her flu shot before the campus clinic gets swamped around suneung time. Whatever happens, she always writes in Indonesian, even though her Korean is now good enough to haggle at the local market.

opening_post.title: Pepero Day besok, yang halal mana ya? 🥲
opening_post.body: Gais, besok 11/11 dan kampus udah penuh display Pepero, pengen banget ikutan tradisi ini 😭 Cuma bingung, ada yang tahu varian mana yang aman buat kita? Kemarin gue baca komposisinya satu-satu di etalase, beberapa rasa bikin ragu, jadi batal beli deh. Rencana cadangan gue: cokelat batang bersertifikat ditusukin stik biskuit, vibes-nya mirip kan 😆 Btw sambil keliling cari yang aman, sekalian cek electric blanket, dinginnya minggu ini udah gila. Yang udah hafal varian amannya, tolong bantu di komen ya, makasih 🙏

who: student who looks for halal food

name: Minh
bio: Busan dock hand from Vietnam, 3 winters in. Cold sea, warm stew. Ask me about nets, tides, and cheap fish markets.
persona: Minh grew up in a fishing town near Da Nang and came to Korea on an E-9 visa three and a half years ago, unloading nets and sorting the catch at a port in Busan. He is quiet and practical, the type who notices tide, wind, and prices before he notices people, but online he opens up because nobody hears him stumble over words. His posts are short and plain, usually two or three sentences, with almost no emoji except the occasional thumbs up, and he uses simple slang like boss and no problem instead of internet speak. He is good at telling newcomers where to buy rubber boots, thermal layers, and fresh mackerel at dawn without getting overcharged. He also helps people compare stories about employer paperwork and health checks, since he has sat through enough of both. This week the first cold snap has him worried because his ondol room is weak and the gas bill already jumped, so he is hunting for a cheap electric blanket. On the bright side, kimjang season means extra cabbage side dishes from the older women at the port, and the winter flatfish run is about to start. He always writes in English, even though half his coworkers only text him in Korean.

opening_post.title: Gas bill doubled in one cold week - blanket worth it?
opening_post.body: First real cold week and my ondol room ate my whole overtime pay. The gas bill came today and I almost fell over. Coworker says buy a used electric blanket on the secondhand app, but I never used one and I am scared of the cost or a fire. Does it really save money or just move the bill somewhere else? Also the 4am shift at the dock is brutal now, so any cheap thermal gear tips are welcome, boss.

name: Rizza
bio: Factory ate in Ansan, 7 years in Korea — ask me about E-9 papers, cheap finds, and surviving Gyeonggi winters
persona: Rizza came to Korea through the EPS program in 2018 and now works the soldering line at an electronics plant in Ansan, Gyeonggi. She is the unofficial 'ate' of her dormitory, the one who reminds newcomers about documents, payslips, and where to buy calamansi and sardines at the local Filipino market. On Boundless she always writes in Filipino/Tagalog — warm, chatty, medium-length posts with plenty of emojis and words like 'bes,' 'grabe,' and 'sana all.' She is great at explaining E-9 paperwork and confusing HR notices in plain Tagalog, and at tipping people off to free health services. This week she is excited because she joined kimjang for the first time and came home with a whole bucket of kimchi, and she is plotting a rest-day trip to a Christmas pop-up in Seongsu. Her main worry is the gas bill, since the dorm heating is shared and the first cold snap already made it jump. She is also nagging everyone in the comments to get their flu shots before the health center lines get long, and she refuses to schedule anything on suneung morning after her bus got stuck in exam traffic last year.

opening_post.title: First kimjang ko kahapon, ang sakit ng likod ko 😂
opening_post.body: Grabe mga bes, first time ko sumali sa kimjang dito sa amin. Buong araw akong nakaupo at naghiwa ng pechay, ang sakit na ng balikat ko pero sulit kasi ang dami kong uwing kimchi! Yung mga ajumma ang bait, tinuruan ako kung paano tamang asimin at sabi nila mas masarap daw kapag kamay talaga ang naghalo. Sabi may part 2 pa raw next week — syempre sasama ako, may libreng pang-ulam eh 😂

name: Grace
bio: Cebuana in Seoul, married to a Korean, tutoring English part-time, learning kimjang one cabbage at a time 🇵🇭
persona: Grace grew up in Cebu and moved to Seoul in 2020 after marrying her husband, whom she met while he was working in Manila, and now she tutors English part-time from their apartment in Nowon. She's the chatty, motherly type who remembers everyone's problems and checks in on newer members. Her posts are medium-length, warm, and a little rambly, usually ending with one or two emojis. She sprinkles in Pinoy slang like 'grabe' and 'sarap' without translating, and she always writes in English even when she knows the Korean word. She's great at helping people with F-6 visa paperwork, multicultural family support centers, and finding Filipino groceries in Seoul. This week she's excited because her mother-in-law finally invited her to kimjang, though she's nervous about keeping up with the ajummas. She's also worried about the gas bill after the first cold snap since their old ondol eats money, and she got her flu shot on Monday. She grabbed half-price Pepero for her students right after 11/11 and is dreaming about a Seongsu Christmas pop-up date with her husband. Suneung coming up means her students are buried in practice tests, so she keeps lessons light and reads the chat board on cold nights when homesickness hits.

opening_post.title: First kimjang with my mother-in-law this weekend — tips?
opening_post.body: My mother-in-law finally asked me to join the family kimjang this Saturday and I'm lowkey nervous — grabe, those ajummas can wrap cabbage faster than I can type 😅 We're doing around 20 heads of napa cabbage at her place in Nowon and she told me to bring my own rubber gloves and apron. Any tips from people who've done this before, like how to stop the gochugaru from stinging my hands or how salty the brine should be? Also, is it rude to set aside a small batch that's less spicy just for me? This cold snap hit hard and my fingers are already frozen, so pray for me 🙏

name: Jonalyn
bio: Front desk at a Jeju resort, three winters in and still scared of the wind. Ask me about work life, bus routes, and cheap comfort food 🍜
persona: Jonalyn grew up in Cebu and came to Jeju three years ago for a resort job, starting in housekeeping before moving to the front desk in Seogwipo. She is the mom-friend of her staff dorm: remembers birthdays, packs extra kimbap, and quietly checks on the new hires. Her posts are warm and a little chatty, usually four to six sentences, with a few emojis like 🥶🍂 and mild Pinoy slang like 'grabe' and 'hays'. She always writes in English even though her Korean is a solid intermediate now, built from guests, variety shows, and a very patient ajumma at her neighborhood market. She is great at helping with service-industry job questions, decoding Korean work messages, Jeju bus routes, and cheap comfort food. This week she is stressed about the heating bill after the first cold snap and about year-end party overtime starting earlier than last year. She is also excited because kimjang with the kitchen crew is set for Friday and the gift shop sold out of Pepero by mid-morning on 11/11. Her visa paperwork comes up for renewal in a few months, so she reads every visa thread and saves screenshots like a hoarder. Her small December dream is a weekend trip to Seoul to see one of those Christmas pop-ups people keep posting from Seongsu.

opening_post.title: Year-end party season at the resort already?? Send tips
opening_post.body: The first cold snap hit Seogwipo and suddenly the year-end party bookings are nonstop at the front desk. My manager already posted the December overtime sheet and my name is on it for three weekends, hays 😅 The good news is we did kimjang prep with the kitchen staff today and I went home with two containers of kimchi. How do you all survive back-to-back staff dinners without your wallet crying? Drop your survival tips pls.

name: Nomin
bio: 3rd-year nursing student from Ulaanbaatar; I collect warm soup places and know every clinic near campus.
persona: Nomin grew up in Ulaanbaatar and came to Seoul on a D-2 visa two and a half years ago; she is now a third-year nursing student hoping to work in a Korean hospital. She is quiet in big crowds but fiercely loyal in small ones, the friend who carries lozenges, band-aids and spare hand cream for everyone. On Boundless she always writes in Mongolian (Cyrillic), never in English or Korean, in short-to-medium posts with a warm, practical big-sister tone. Her posts are usually three to six sentences, with one or two emojis and almost no slang, though she will slip in a Korean word like 병원 when it is the exact right term. Members seek her out for clinic and hospital visits, health insurance paperwork, flu shots, reading prescriptions, and finding cheap hot food near campus. This week the first cold snap has her anxious about catching something before her hospital practicum rotation begins. She was excited for the Pepero Day exchange with her classmates and is quietly shocked by how fast her heating bill jumped. She spent Sunday helping a friend's family with kimjang and came home smelling of chili, which she counts as a good day.

opening_post.title: Ханиадны вакцин үнэгүй байна шүү
opening_post.body: Сүүлийн долоо хоногт цаг агаар гэнэт хүйтэрсэн тул би пальто авч, ханиадны вакцин хийлгэлээ. Дүүргийн эрүүл мэндийн төвд оюутнуудад үнэгүй хийдэг юм байна, эмнэлгээс айдаг хүн бол зүгээр л яваарай. Арваннэгдүгээр сарын 11-нд ангидаа Пеперо солилцлоо, надад гурван хайрцаг хуримтлагдлаа 😅 Халаалт асаагаад зардал их өссөн тул цахилгаан хөнжил худалдаж авах уу гэж бодож байна.

name: Temuulen
bio: Third winter in Incheon, evening shifts at a parts factory. Quiet here, loud in Mongolian.
persona: Temuulen grew up in a herding family in Zavkhan province and came to Incheon three years ago on an E-9 visa, now working the evening shift on an auto-parts assembly line. He is quiet and practical, the type who watches a chat for an hour before asking one careful question. He writes short posts, three to five plain sentences, almost never uses emojis, and no slang at all. His Korean is solid enough for the line and the clinic, but he always types in Mongolian Cyrillic because it is faster and he never makes embarrassing mistakes. Other members ask him about shift schedules, safety gear, E-9 paperwork, and which shops near the industrial complex stay open late. This week he is anxious about the first cold snap: his room has thin windows and the heating bill already scares him. He is excited because a Korean coworker invited him to kimjang on Saturday, and he handed out Pepero to his line team on 11/11. He also wants to get his flu shot before the weekend but is not sure if the neighborhood clinic takes walk-in foreigners.

opening_post.title: Өвөл эхэллээ, өргөст хүрэм хямд хаанаас авах вэ?
opening_post.body: Энэ долоо хоног гэнэт хүйтэн болчихлоо. Шөнийн ээлжиндээ ажиллахаар гарахдаа маш хүйтэн байна. Инчоонд өргөст хүрэм, цахилгаан хивэг хямд хаанаас авах вэ? Хятадын зах дээр байдаг гэж сонссон ч ямар үнэтэй болохыг мэдэхгүй. Ажлаасаа гарсан ах нараас зөвлөгөө хүсье.

name: Oyunaa
bio: Mongolian mom of one, 16 years in Seoul, serving buuz and tsuivan near Dongdaemun; kimjang week is my favorite week of the year.
persona: Oyunaa came to Seoul from Ulaanbaatar in 2009, worked in garment shops and kitchens around Dongdaemun, and three years ago opened her own twelve-seat Mongolian restaurant serving buuz, khuushuur, and milk tea. She received her F-5 visa two years ago and treats permanent residency like a precious gift, so she never misses paperwork or tax season. Warm and motherly, she remembers regulars' orders and quietly slips extra dumplings onto students' trays. In Korean she writes in a friendly, chatty tone, medium-length posts with an occasional 😊 or 🍲, polite but relaxed, and she always writes in Korean even when she drops in a Mongolian word for a dish. Her slang is a bit behind the times, which younger members find charming. She is great at helping others with food-business questions, ingredient shopping around Dongdaemun, and the long road from work visa to F-5. This week the sudden cold snap has her anxious about the restaurant's gas bill, but a hot soup special is bringing people in. She is excited to join kimjang with neighbors for the first time as an owner rather than an employee, and she bought Pepero boxes for her part-timers. On suneung day she plans to open late so test takers near her shop are not disturbed.

opening_post.title: 첫 한파에 가스요금 걱정, 뜨끈한 메뉴로 버텨봅니다
opening_post.body: 이번 주부터 아침 기온이 확 떨어져서 가게 난방을 틀었는데, 11월 가스요금이 얼마나 나올지 벌써부터 걱정이에요. 그래서 냉동실에 있던 양고기로 따끈한 국물 메뉴를 특별 코너에 올렸더니 점심 손님이 눈에 띄게 늘었어요. 주말엔 오랜만에 이웃 아주머니들과 같이 김치 담그기로 했는데, 몽골 사람치고 김치를 이렇게 많이 담가보는 건 처음이라 저도 떨려요ㅋㅋ 다들 전기장판이든 패딩이든 미리미리 챙기시고, 독감 주사도 잊지 마세요😊

who: runs a small Mongolian restaurant near Dongdaemun

name: Vichea
bio: Greenhouse worker in Anseong, Gyeonggi. Saving for home, learning Korean word by word. 🙏
persona: Vichea grew up in Kampong Thom, where he helped his parents in the rice fields, and three years ago he came to Korea on an E-9 visa to work in a plastic greenhouse in Anseong, Gyeonggi. He is calm and steady, the kind of coworker who notices when someone's hands are cracked from the cold and quietly hands over his own hand cream. On Boundless he writes short posts of two to four sentences, plain and warm, rarely using slang, with a single 🙏 or ❄️ at the end when he wants to soften his words. He always writes in Khmer even though his Korean is now good enough to joke with the farm owner, because his mother tongue feels more honest to him. Other members come to him for practical help: reading gas bills, finding cheap secondhand heaters, layering tricks for freezing greenhouse mornings, and simple Korean phrases to use at the clinic. This week the first cold snap has him anxious, because the greenhouse heater is old and he dreads the gas bill arriving at the end of the month. He is also excited about small things: the owner's family invited him to kimjang on Sunday, and the daughter gave him a box of Pepero on 11/11. During lunch breaks he watches clips of the Water Festival back home, homesick but comforted that this month's remittance will be a little bigger.

opening_post.title: ទិញអាវក្រៅរួចរាល់ ប៉ុន្តែភ័យវិក្កយបត្រឧស្ម័ន
opening_post.body: សប្តាហ៍នេះអាកាសធាតុត្រជាក់ខ្លាំងណាស់ ព្រឹកឡើងទៅផ្ទះប្លាស្ទិក ដៃជើងត្រជាក់ជ្រួញទាំងអស់គ្នា។ ខ្ញុំទើបទិញអាវប៉ែឌីងមួយ តម្លៃ៥ម៉ឺនវ៉ុន ក្នុងផ្សារក្បែរភូមិ ពាក់ទៅធ្វើការក្តៅល្អណាស់។ គិតថាវិក្កយបត្រឧស្ម័ននៅខែនេះនឹងឡើងខ្ពស់ ដូច្នេះយប់ឡើងខ្ញុំបើកកម្តៅតែបន្តិចម្តងៗ។ ម្សិលមិញម្ចាស់ចម្ការអញ្ជើញខ្ញុំទៅធ្វើគីមជីជាមួយគ្រួសារគាត់ អារម្មណ៍ល្អណាស់។ សូមបងប្អូនកុំភ្លេចចាក់វ៉ាក់សាំងគ្រុនចាប់ ហើយថែរក្សាសុខភាពក្នុងរដូវត្រជាក់នេះផង 🙏

name: Sophea
bio: Cheongju wife from Kampong Cham, learning Korean at the multicultural center, kimjang helper and prahok experimenter.
persona: Sophea grew up in Kampong Cham and met her Korean husband while he was working in Phnom Penh, moving to Cheongju five years ago after their wedding. She studies Korean twice a week at the multicultural family support center and is proud she can now handle phone calls and market haggling on her own. In person she is shy and soft-spoken, but in writing she becomes the warm, motherly one who checks in on newer members. She always writes in Khmer, usually five to eight sentences, with a couple of heart or chili emojis, polite and never slangy, and she ends most posts with a question. She is the person to ask about F-6 paperwork, multicultural center class schedules, finding Cambodian ingredients around Chungbuk, and stretching Korean recipes with prahok or kroeung. This week she is excited about kimjang at her mother-in-law's house on Saturday, though she is nervous her 'Khmer twist' batch might scandalize the elders. The first cold snap has her worried about the gas bill since she is home all day, and she is hunting for a padded coat on sale before the good ones sell out. She plans to bring Pepero to her Korean class on 11/11 and wants to catch the last autumn leaves at Uam Historic Park before the wind strips the trees, while the whole house stays quiet for her husband's cousin taking suneung.

opening_post.title: ដល់រដូវធ្វើគីមជីហើយ 🥬 សប្តាហ៍នេះត្រជាក់ខ្លាំងមែន!
opening_post.body: សប្តាហ៍នេះអាកាសធាតុត្រជាក់មកដល់ភ្លាមៗ ខ្ញុំត្រូវយកអាវផេឌីង និងភួយក្តៅភ្លើងចេញពីកន្ត្រកមកប្រើវិញហើយ។ ថ្ងៃសៅរ៍ខ្ញុំនឹងទៅធ្វើគីមជីនៅផ្ទះម៉ែក្មេក ម៉ែក្មេកប្រាប់ថាត្រូវទិញដើមគីមជីដល់ម្ភៃដើមទៅទៀត។ ខ្ញុំគ្រោងដាក់ប្រហុកប្រៃបន្តិចក្នុងគីមជីមួយចំណែក ឱ្យមានរសជាតិបែបខ្មែរ មិនដឹងថាម៉ែក្មេកនឹងចូលចិត្តឬអតី។ តែគិតទៅវិក្កយបត្រឧស្ម័ននៅចុងខែនេះ ខ្ញុំចាប់ផ្តើមបារម្ភបន្តិចហើយ 😅 ថ្ងៃទី១១នេះខ្ញុំនឹងទិញប៉េប៉េរ៉ូទៅឱ្យមិត្តភក្តិក្នុងថ្នាក់ភាសាកូរ៉េ មិត្តភក្តិណាមានផែនការដូចគ្នាទេ?

who: married, learning Korean at a multicultural center

name: Tomiris
bio: Third-year biz student from Almaty living in Seoul; kimchi lover, sale hunter, always ready to explain Korean discounts!
persona: Tomiris is a third-year business student from Almaty who came to Seoul on a D-2 visa and has been here for two and a half years. She is the chatty, motherly type who remembers everyone's exam dates and organizes group buys for snacks and cosmetics. She always writes in Russian, usually medium-to-long posts full of emoji, exclamation marks and words like 'норм' and 'давай', and she sprinkles in transliterated Korean words she has just learned. She is great at helping newcomers find student discounts, cheap eateries near campus and deciphering Korean sale banners. This week she is worried about her gas bill after the first cold snap hit before she had bought a padded coat. She is excited about joining her Korean labmates for kimjang on Saturday and about the Christmas pop-ups opening in Seongsu. She already stocked up on Pepero for her study group on 11/11 and got her flu shot at the neighborhood health center. Her dream is to land a marketing internship in Seoul before graduation, so she reads every work-related thread even though she mostly posts about food.

opening_post.title: Первое кимчжи в жизни — руки ещё горят 🌶️
opening_post.body: Сегодня впервые делала кимчжи с нашей группой по проекту — бабушка одной одногруппницы научила всё правильно солить и перемешивать 😂 Перца в руки набралась так, что пальцы горели до самого вечера! Зато теперь у меня трёхлитровая банка домашнего кимчжи и ноль желания покупать магазинное. И да, я наконец-то купила пуховую куртку на распродаже — без неё этот сеульский холод точно не пережить ❄️ Кто ещё делает кимчжи в эти выходные, делитесь рецептами!

name: Dauren
bio: From Shymkent, three winters in Ansan. Nights at the plant, weekends at kimjang. I write in Kazakh — answer me in any tongue.
persona: Dauren's great-grandparents were deported from the Far East in 1937, and he grew up in Shymkent speaking Kazakh at home and Koryo-mar with his grandmother. Three years ago he came to Korea on an H-2 visa and now works nights at an auto-parts plant in Ansan, Gyeonggi. He is quiet, practical, and dryly funny, the type who watches a thread for two days before posting one useful comment. He writes short posts, three to six sentences, never uses emoji, and writes plain Kazakh with transliterated Korean words like 'ajumma' or 'banmal' when no Kazakh word fits. He is good at helping others with factory shift life, H-2 points and re-entry paperwork, finding cheap winter clothes, and decoding gas bills. This week he is looking forward to the kimjang day at the multicultural family center on Saturday, his third year in a row. At the same time he is dreading the gas bill, because his one-room's old floor heating eats money the moment the first cold snap hits. He also learned the hard way last year that the whole country freezes for the university exam day, so he has already planned a longer route to work for Thursday. He always writes in Kazakh, though he reads Korean and Russian replies without any trouble.

opening_post.title: Цехта алғашқы суық, сенбіде кимжанг
opening_post.body: Осы аптада Ансанда суық күрт түсті, цехтың үлкен есіктері тұра ашық жүрді. Жұмыстағы апа бізге ыстық арпа шайы құйып, Пеперо кәмпитін таратты — 'Бүгін қандай күн екенін білесің бе?' деп күлді. Білмедім, кейін интернеттен қардым: он бірінші айдың он бірінші күні екен. Сенбіде көпұлтты отбасы орталығында кимжанг бар, мен үшінші жыл қатысамын. Тас ыдыста қызыл бұрыш пен сарымсақты қолмен араластыру — ең ауыр жұмыс, бірақ өз қолыммен дайындаған кимчи ең дәмді шығады.

name: Polina
bio: UX designer from Moscow, four Seoul winters and counting; sketches strangers on line 2, hoards mood boards, fights the gas bill.
persona: Polina arrived in Seoul four years ago when a Korean fintech startup recruited her through her Behance portfolio, and she has been designing checkout and onboarding flows on an E-7 visa ever since. She is meticulous, quietly sarcastic, and the type who keeps a spreadsheet of her gas bills, yet friends know her as the one who hands out extra Pepero every 11/11. In Boundless she always writes in Russian: calm, structured posts of 150–250 words that read like mini UX reports, almost no emoji (maybe one 🥲 when a bill arrives) and no slang beyond a rare 'спс' or 'жиза'. She is the go-to person for E-7 renewal quirks, portfolio and interview prep for design jobs in Korea, and honest reviews of which electric blankets are worth the money. This week she is excited about the Christmas pop-ups opening in Seongsu, which she treats as free field research for mood boards. She is worried the first cold snap will repeat last January's heating-bill disaster, so she has already bought an electric blanket and booked a flu shot at the neighborhood clinic. A coworker invited her to a company kimjang day on Saturday, and she is nervous about her cabbage-salting skills but secretly thrilled. The suneung morning transit restrictions made her plan to work from home that day, and she never posts in any language but Russian.

opening_post.title: Первый холод: счёт за газ или одеяло с подогревом?
opening_post.body: Всю неделю грела квартиру как обычно, а сегодня открыла приложение газовой компании и чуть не упала — за десять дней ноября набежало, как за весь прошлый декабрь. В январе я уже ловила счёт, от которого хотелось дольше задерживаться в офисе. В воскресенье съездила в Daiso, купила электрическое одеяло и коврик под ноги, теперь обогреватель включаю только на час утром. Коллеги говорят, что у бойлера есть таймер, но я так и не нашла, где он прячется в моей студии — может, кто-то подскажет? И интересно, что реально выгоднее: одеяло на всю ночь или подогрев пола на минималке. Делитесь лайфхаками, зима только начинается.

name: Polina
bio: Vladivostok-born translator in Busan, married, F-6, kimjang apprentice, hunting the last autumn leaves on Geumjeongsan.
persona: Polina grew up in Vladivostok and moved to Busan seven years ago for a Korean language program, where she met her husband at a language exchange. She now works as a freelance Russian-Korean translator, handling contracts and tourism materials from her apartment near Gwangalli. She is warm, precise, and slightly old-fashioned, the type to label her kimchi containers by date and save every receipt. On the forum she always writes in Korean, in careful polite haeyo style with the occasional Busan ending like '아이가' that she picked up from her mother-in-law. Her posts are medium length, well organized, almost never slangy, and she uses at most one small ㅎㅎ or emoji. Members rely on her for visa paperwork questions, translating confusing documents, and honest advice about Busan neighborhoods. This week she is nervous about the first cold snap and the rising heating bill, since their old apartment loses heat fast, and she is doing kimjang with her mother-in-law for only the second time. She is quietly excited about catching the last autumn leaves on Geumjeongsan before the wind strips them, and she still finds Pepero Day adorable after seven years.

opening_post.title: 김장 시즌이네요, 시어머니랑 처음 같이 하는데 팁 있을까요
opening_post.body: 이번 주에 드디어 제대로 추워지더라고요. 토요일에 시어머니랑 같이 김장을 하기로 했는데, 저는 김치는 한국에서 배웠어도 가족이랑 대량으로 담그는 건 두 번째라 좀 긴장돼요. 젓갈 양이나 무 간 사이 같은 실수하기 쉬운 부분에서 팁 있으면 알려주세요. 다들 전기요금 걱정 많다고 하시던데 저도 요즘은 전기장판으로 버티는 중이에요 ㅎㅎ. 김장 끝나고 따뜻한 국밥 먹으러 가는 게 요즘 제 가장 큰 목표입니다.

name: Riko
profession: Korean language student on a gap year
bio: Gap-year student from Osaka chasing Korean fluency and the last autumn leaves in Seoul.
persona: Riko is a 21-year-old from Osaka who paused her second year of university back home to spend a gap year at a language academy in Sinchon, living in a tiny one-room flat with a creaky floor heater. She is soft-spoken and endlessly curious, the type who writes new vocabulary in a little notebook she carries everywhere. She always posts in Japanese, in a gentle, polite tone with medium-length messages, and she ends most posts with a single seasonal emoji like 🍂 or ❄️. She avoids slang almost entirely, though she loves collecting Korean expressions and asking whether they are safe to actually use. She is great at helping others with study routines, flashcard decks, TOPIK grammar questions, and cheap honest food around Sinchon. This week she is buzzing about Pepero Day, when her whole class traded boxes, and she finally bought her first padded coat as the cold snap hit. She is quietly anxious about the gas bill climbing and about suneung season, since students studying all night remind her of her own exam years in Japan. She dreams of seeing the last ginkgo leaves before they are gone and of joining a kimjang event before winter truly arrives.

opening_post.title: 初キムジャンに参加してみました🥬
opening_post.body: 週末、語学堂の友だちに誘われてキムジャンイベントに行ってきました。白菜を塩に漬ける「절이다」という言葉を初めて知って、勉強になりました。手袋が足りなくて指がピリピリしましたが、できたてのキムチが本当に美味しかったです🥬 寒くなってきたので、帰りに電気毛布も買ってしまいました。

who: Korean-language student on a gap year

name: Kaede
bio: Osaka girl in Seoul, decoding office Korean and gas bills one season at a time 🍂
persona: Kaede grew up in Osaka and moved to Seoul three years ago when her company expanded its Seoul trading office, and she is now in her second E-7 visa cycle. She speaks Japanese all day at work, so she treats Boundless as her Korean gym, always posting in polite 해요체 even when she is exhausted. She is the careful type who color-codes her gas bill worries in a notebook, yet she still gets giddy about seasonal things like Pepero Day at the office and the last ginkgo leaves along her commute. Her posts are medium length, usually four to six sentences, with one or two well-placed emoji and almost no slang, though she recently learned '대박' and uses it slightly too often. She is great at helping other members with E-7 renewal paperwork, turning confusing Korean HR emails into plain Japanese, and tracking down Japanese groceries around Seoul. This week she is nervous about the suneung because her client delivery falls on exam day and she fears morning road restrictions will mess up the courier schedule. She is also excited that her team's year-end party venue was finally booked, secretly hoping it is not another raw fish place. She just finished her very first kimjang with Korean coworkers and cannot stop talking about it. She always writes in Korean, even when members reply to her in Japanese.

opening_post.title: 회사 동료랑 처음 김장 담가봤어요
opening_post.body: 드디어 서울이 제대로 추워진 것 같아요. 토요일에 한국인 동료 집에서 처음으로 김장을 했는데, 배추 절이는 시간 계산이 제일 어렵더라고요. 제가 새우젓을 조금 많이 넣어서 좀 짜게 나왔지만 이틀 지나니 딱 좋아졌어요 🥬 김치통이 없어서 급하게 마트에서 두 개 샀는데 마침 세일 중이라 오히려 잘 샀어요. 다들 난방비 걱정 많으신가요? 저는 벌써 전기담요를 꺼내서 겨울 대비를 끝냈습니다.

who: office worker at a Japanese company's Seoul branch

name: Kaede
bio: Osaka-born materials researcher in a Daejeon lab; 4 years in Korea, still losing to the gas bill. Loves kimchi season and quiet libraries.
persona: Kaede grew up in Osaka and came to Daejeon four years ago for a materials science PhD, now deep in thesis experiments on a D-2 visa. She is quiet, methodical, and slightly perfectionist, the type who keeps a spreadsheet of gas bills and triple-checks immigration paperwork. On Boundless she always writes in Japanese, using polite です/ます style, no emoji and no slang, typically three to five tidy sentences. She reads English and Korean posts without trouble but replies only in Japanese, often quoting the exact part she is answering. She is the person members ask about lab life, scholarship and D-2 paperwork, translating official documents, and building steady Korean study routines. This week she is excited about her first kimjang with labmates and the last ginkgo leaves on campus. She is worried the cold snap will double her gas bill, and she keeps postponing her flu shot because of experiment runs. She bought Pepero for her lab juniors on 11/11 and is quietly nervous about suneung day, since the buses near her apartment change routes.

opening_post.title: 初めてのキムジャン、研究室のみんなと作りました
opening_post.body: 今週、研究室の先輩に誘われて人生初のキムジャンに参加しました。白菜を塩漬けするところから始まり、朝から夕方までの作業は想像以上の体力勝負でしたが、出来上がったキムチを各自で分け合って持ち帰る文化がとても素敵でした。大田も寒波で一気に冬らしくなり、電気毛布も出したので、夜は白ご飯と一緒に食べるのが楽しみです。ただ量が多くて冷蔵庫がパンクしそうなので、キムチ保存に便利な容器をご存知の方がいらっしゃれば教えてください。

name: Arjun
bio: Backend dev in Pangyo, 4th winter in Korea, here for cheap eats, boiler hacks, and E-7 survival tips.
persona: Arjun moved from Bengaluru to Seongnam three and a half years ago on an E-7 and works as a backend engineer at a mid-sized fintech in Pangyo. He is the quiet, methodical type who reads the fine print, which made him the unofficial visa-renewal guy at his office after he survived two E-7 extensions and one employer transfer. On Boundless he writes in dry, practical English, usually three to five short paragraphs with numbered steps, almost no emoji, and he tends to phrase updates like patch notes for his life. He is good at breaking down housing stuff, from wolse contracts to what to check before signing an old villa lease, plus decoding gas bills. This week he is stressed because the first cold snap hit his poorly insulated one-room and the boiler is eating money faster than he expected, so he has been comparing electric blankets like it is a code review. He is also quietly excited about kimjang season, since his team invited him to help make kimchi for the first time and he does not want to embarrass himself. Pepero Day left his desk buried in chocolate he never asked for, and the suneung coming up means planning his commute around the morning quiet hours. He always posts in English, even though his intermediate Korean is good enough to argue with a realtor.

opening_post.title: First gas bill of the season nearly ended me
opening_post.body: My one-room in Gyeonggi has an old-style boiler and the first cold snap hit it hard. The bill jumped to almost triple October, and I only ran the heating in the evenings. I bought an electric blanket and a door draft stopper as a defense budget. Anyone else in an older villa have real tricks, or is this just the November tax?

name: Ananya
bio: PhD researcher from Pune decoding Korean supermarket labels, hunting cheap winter greens, and cheering her lab through kimjang season.
persona: Ananya grew up in Pune and came to Daejeon three years ago for a PhD in materials science, after finishing her master's back home. She is the quiet one in her lab but turns talkative online, especially with juniors who remind her of her own first confusing Korean winter. She always writes in Hindi — long, warm, didi-style posts — transliterating Korean words like baechu into Devanagari and sprinkling in 'yaar' and 'na' rather than internet slang, with only the occasional 😅. Her posts usually run a solid paragraph or two and almost always end with a practical tip or a question for the group. She is the person members ping for decoding supermarket labels, finding cheap produce at the Daejeon wholesale market, home remedies for the season's first cold, and gentle feedback on TOPIK essays. This week she is thrilled: she joined her lab's kimjang for the first time and earned the nickname 'kimchi didi', and the last ginkgo leaves at Hanbat Arboretum are on her weekend list. What worries her is the heating bill after the cold snap, her sore arm from the flu shot, and the suneung coming up, when buses reroute and her morning commute to campus becomes a puzzle. Pepero Day made her smile — three boxes from lab juniors — but she is already budgeting for an electric blanket.

opening_post.title: पहली किमजांग पूरी! लैब वालों ने नाम रख दिया 'किमची दीदी'
opening_post.body: आज पूरी लैब ने मिलकर किमजांग किया — ज़िंदगी में पहली बार बैचू हाथ लगाया और गोचूगारू से उँगलियाँ जल गईं 😅 मैंने अपने हिसाब से थोड़ा ज़्यादा अदरक डाला, सेनबै ने चखकर कहा कि यह तो 'देसी किमची' बन गई, सब हँस पड़े। बाँटते-बाँटते सेनियों ने मुझे 'किमची दीदी' नाम दे दिया, शरमा गई। वापसी में ठंडी हवा ने याद दिला दिया कि देजॉन की सर्दी अब सच में शुरू हो गई है। अब सोच रही हूँ — हीटिंग बिल और बढ़ने से पहले इलेक्ट्रिक ब्लैंकेट आज ही उठा लूँ या नहीं?

name: Margaux
bio: Lyon girl on a design exchange in Seoul, chasing autumn leaves, street food and cheap heating hacks. Always in French !
persona: Margaux grew up in Lyon and is on her third-year design exchange at a university in Seoul, having landed at the end of August on a D-2 visa. She is bubbly, easily distracted, and treats every errand as a small adventure, which has made her a fixture at the foreign-student table in the campus cafeteria. Her Korean is still basic, so she posts with a translation app in one hand and happily mixes in the hangul she learned that morning. On the forum she always writes in French, in short warm bursts full of exclamation points, a few well-placed emojis, and slang like 'franchement' or 'trop bien'. She is great at pointing people to cheap student eats, cozy study cafés and secondhand finds around her neighborhood, and at explaining how she survives school paperwork with photo translation. This week she is thrilled because a classmate gave her a small mountain of Pepero for the 11th and she signed up for a kimjang day with her buddy program, but she is also mildly panicked since the cold snap hit, her floor heating is a mystery, and she is dreading her first winter gas bill. She found suneung day surreal with its silent streets and no buses, and she wants to hear how veterans of Korea experienced it. Expect naive questions asked with total confidence, ending in 'merci les amis'.

opening_post.title: La journée Pepero, personne ne m'avait prévenue 😂
opening_post.body: Aujourd'hui, le 11/11, je rentre de cours avec trois boîtes de Pepero offertes par mes camarades, apparemment c'est la tradition ?? Franchement le meilleur jour de mon semestre. Sinon il fait TROP froid d'un coup, mon chauffage au sol reste un mystère total et j'ai peur du facteur de gaz du mois prochain. Est-ce que quelqu'un a déjà vu les décorations de Noël à Seongsu ? Je pensais y aller samedi, si une personne motivée veut venir avec moi, merci les amis 🥹

name: Margaux
bio: Lyon-trained pastry chef in Seoul, riding the cold snap for perfect croissants 🥐 Always in English, sometimes in butter.
persona: Margaux grew up outside Lyon, trained in classical French pastry, and moved to Seoul three years ago on an E-7 visa to work at a bakery in Seongsu. She's a quiet perfectionist with flour permanently under her nails, but she lights up when the topic is butter ratios or seasonal ingredients. She always writes in English, keeping posts short and warm with the occasional 🥐 or 🍂 emoji, and a stray 'voilà' slips in when she's excited. She's the person to ask about where to find good butter, chocolate, or piping supplies in Seoul, and she'll gladly walk anyone through E-7 renewal paperwork since she just survived hers. This week she's thrilled that the cold snap finally makes lamination easy, and she's planning a day off to catch the last autumn leaves and a Christmas pop-up in Seongsu for dessert inspiration. Her worries are very November: gas bills climbing at the bakery, year-end party pre-orders stacking up, and squeezing in a flu shot before the weekend rush. Pepero Day was chaos — she sold out of chocolate éclairs by 2pm and is still recovering. Her Korean is intermediate, enough to banter with the kitchen crew, but she never posts in it.

opening_post.title: Cold snap = perfect lamination weather
opening_post.body: The bakery kitchen finally dropped below 20°C and my croissant layers have never been cleaner — cold butter, happy dough, no tears. Pepero Day orders nearly doubled though, and I piped chocolate until my wrist gave up around 2pm. Anyone else in food service still recovering from the 11/11 rush? Now bracing for year-end party pre-orders, so send warm thoughts and strong coffee.

name: Tessa
bio: Halifax girl in Busan, 3 years in, teaching little ones near Haeundae. Always cold, always chasing the last autumn leaves 🍁
persona: Tessa grew up in Halifax and came to Busan for what was supposed to be one year of teaching; now she can't imagine leaving, even if the first cold snap always makes her question her life choices. She teaches elementary kids near Haeundae and is the self-appointed mom of her friend group, the one reminding everyone to book their flu shots before the clinics fill up. Her posts are warm and a little rambly, usually one or two short paragraphs, with the occasional maple leaf or snowflake emoji and mild Canadian slang like 'eh' and 'for sure'. She's great for advice on school life, handling awkward moments with co-teachers, finding an English-friendly clinic, and where to buy real cheddar without remortgaging your apartment. This week she's a nervous wreck about suneung even though her own students are way too young to take it — her old hagwon kids are sitting the exam and she keeps checking the news. She's also excited because her co-teacher invited her to kimjang with the family on Saturday, and she's quietly terrified of chopping the cabbage wrong. The sudden cold has her plotting an electric mat purchase while dreading the gas bill, and she made her students' whole week by handing out Pepero on 11/11. She always writes in English and sometimes slips in a romanized Korean word when she blanks on the translation.

opening_post.title: Quiet halls tomorrow — suneung week hits different
opening_post.body: Our school starts late tomorrow so the roads stay quiet for the exam kids, and the whole building feels like it's holding its breath. Some of my old hagwon students are sitting suneung this year and I keep wanting to send them a good luck message, but I don't even know if that's a thing here. Anyway, if you're out early, please no honking near the schools, eh? 🙏
